date.note: Issued in numerous part-volumes between 1932 (when the first half-volume, I/1, appeared) and 1967, and left unfinished at Karl Barth's death in 1968. The German original (Die Kirchliche Dogmatik) comprises thirteen part-volumes across four volumes; the standard English translation was published by T. & T. Clark (Edinburgh) between 1936 and 1977. The year 1932 marks the first part-volume, not a single date of completion.

summary: The Church Dogmatics (Kirchliche Dogmatik) is the unfinished multi-volume systematic theology of the Swiss Reformed theologian Karl Barth, issued in thirteen part-volumes between 1932 and 1967 and left incomplete at his death. Organized around the self-revelation of God in Jesus Christ, it treats dogmatics as the church's critical self-examination of its talk about God, takes the Word of God as the ground and object of theology, and recasts the doctrine of election christologically; it is widely regarded as a central work of twentieth-century Protestant theology.
description:
The Church Dogmatics (Die Kirchliche Dogmatik) is the major work of Karl Barth (1886-1968), the Swiss Reformed theologian widely treated as the most influential Protestant theologian of the twentieth century. Barth issued it in a long sequence of part-volumes from 1932 onward and continued working on it until near his death in 1968, leaving it unfinished; the German original runs to thirteen part-volumes grouped into four volumes (I, the doctrine of the Word of God; II, the doctrine of God; III, the doctrine of creation; IV, the doctrine of reconciliation), with the projected fifth volume on redemption never written. The standard English translation, edited by G. W. Bromiley and T. F. Torrance, was published by T. & T. Clark between 1936 and 1977.

In its opening volume Barth defines the scope and method of the enterprise. He presents dogmatics not as a free speculative system but as a function of the church: the discipline by which the church critically examines and measures its own proclamation, its talk about God, against the standard of the Word of God to which it is bound. On this account theology is a churchly and a critical activity, a self-examination rather than a construction of general truths about religion. Barth orders the whole around the Word of God, which he presents in a threefold form (revealed in Jesus Christ, written in Scripture, and preached in the church's proclamation), and treats the Word of God as at once the ground and the object of theology, so that God is known only where God gives himself to be known in his self-revelation and not by way of an independent natural theology; his sharp rejection of natural theology and of analogia entis in favor of an analogy of faith is a defining and much-discussed feature of the work.

In the second volume, in the doctrine of God, Barth undertakes the christological recasting of the doctrine of election for which the Church Dogmatics is especially known. Against the Reformed tradition of a double decree fixing the eternal destinies of individuals apart from Christ, Barth presents election as God's gracious self-determination in Jesus Christ: Jesus Christ is understood as both the electing God and the elected human being, the one in whom God chooses fellowship with humanity and takes rejection upon himself. Scholarship treats this revision as among Barth's most distinctive and debated moves. The fourth volume, on reconciliation, develops his christocentric account of the atonement and of the covenant of grace at great length and is which some scholars regard as the summit of the work. Across its volumes the Church Dogmatics is marked by close engagement with Scripture, the Reformed and wider confessional heritage, and the history of doctrine, and by its concentration of theology on Jesus Christ. This entry attributes these positions (the definition of dogmatics as churchly self-examination, the theology of the Word of God, the rejection of natural theology, and the christological doctrine of election) to Barth and to the work, and records the work's standing in twentieth-century Protestant theology as a matter of scholarly report, without endorsing or adjudicating its claims.
editorial_notes:
This entry describes the Church Dogmatics on Christian terms (neutrality #1, #4, #6) and attributes its theological claims to Karl Barth and to the work itself. Barth's definition of dogmatics as the church's self-examination of its proclamation, his theology of the Word of God as ground and object of theology, his rejection of natural theology, and his christological recasting of election are stated as his attributed positions, not endorsed or adjudicated; the work's centrality to twentieth-century Protestant theology is reported as scholarly assessment, not as the editor's verdict.

The Theological Declaration of Barmen, 1934. English translation, Thesis 1, confessing 'Jesus Christ, as he is attested to us in Holy Scripture, is the one Word of God whom we have to hear, and whom we have to trust and obey in life and in death,' and its rejection of the false doctrine that the Church could recognize 'other events, powers, historic figures and truths' as God's revelation. Read directly for this entry. Barth was the principal drafter; cited as an open Barth primary for the christocentric concentration of revelation continuous with the Church Dogmatics, not as evidence for the volume-by-volume content of the Dogmatics itself.
